position: Congressional Action Items (Cap indirect costs at universities)
proposal: The Mandate recommends that Congress cap the indirect (overhead) cost rate the federal government pays universities for research so that it does not exceed the lowest rate a university accepts from a private organization funding research. It presents this as a market-based way to reduce federal subsidy of university overhead.

status_summary: No statute capping university indirect cost rates at a private-funder benchmark has been enacted; instead the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75, signed 2026-02-03) continued the bar on HHS developing or implementing a modified approach to indirect cost rates (Div. B sec. 224, per CRS), and a grants consultancy summary reports that it also requires DoD to keep its existing rate framework (Div. A sec. 8146). The executive branch pursued a different design, flat 15 percent caps: NIH issued NOT-OD-25-068 on 2025-02-07, DOE, NSF and DoD issued similar caps in April to June 2025, and courts blocked all four (NIH permanent injunction 2025-04-04, affirmed by the First Circuit on 2026-01-05; DOE preliminary injunction 2025-05-15; NSF policy vacated 2025-06-20; DoD preliminary injunction 2025-07-18), with ACE reporting on 2026-04-13 that the Justice Department did not seek Supreme Court review of the NIH ruling. The FY2027 budget again proposes a 15 percent NIH cap and removal of the bar. Because Congress, the actor the text names, enacted provisions that keep negotiated rates in place rather than a cap, the record is judged diverged.

timeline.event: NIH issued supplemental guidance NOT-OD-25-068 setting a 15 percent indirect cost rate for new and existing grants to institutions of higher education, for costs from 2025-02-10.
The D. Mass. court converted its preliminary relief into a permanent nationwide injunction against the NIH policy.
A federal judge in Massachusetts issued a nationwide preliminary injunction against the DOE 15 percent cap, replacing a temporary restraining order of 2025-04-16.
A D. Mass. judge granted summary judgment vacating the NSF 15 percent rate policy as arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.
A D. Mass. judge issued a preliminary injunction against the DoD 15 percent cap, limited to the named universities and members of ACE, AAU and APLU.

The First Circuit affirmed the NIH ruling (Massachusetts v. NIH, No. 25-1343, with two related appeals), relying on recurring HHS appropriations language and on the Uniform Guidance as adopted at 45 CFR Part 75.
The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 became Public Law 119-75; per CRS, Division B section 224 continues the bar on HHS developing or implementing a modified approach to indirect cost rates.

A grants consultancy summary reported that P.L. 119-75 also requires DoD to keep applying its existing indirect cost rate framework and bars use of funds to change those rates (Div. A sec. 8146), alongside the HHS bar in Div. B sec. 224.
ACE reported that the Justice Department did not file a Supreme Court petition by its April 2026 deadline, leaving the First Circuit decision in place.
CRS reported that P.L. 119-75 continues the HHS indirect cost bar and that the FY2027 budget again proposes a 15 percent NIH cap and removal of the bar.

title: Cap federal indirect cost rates for university research at the lowest private-funder rate
uncertainties: The Mandate asks Congress for a cap tied to the lowest rate a university accepts from a private funder; the 15 percent caps are a flat executive cap and are tracked as a parallel design. The section 224 citation rests on CRS and the section 8146 DoD provision rests on a consultancy summary; on 2026-10-13 the GovInfo HTML and PDF of P.L. 119-75 loaded only through Division A section 8072, so neither provision was read in statutory text. The ACE page is an advocacy-group tracker and is the only source for the NSF and DoD dates and for the absence of a Supreme Court petition. The stage is a judgment call: blocked 10 is the alternative if the court-halted parallel executive caps are treated as the deciding action, while diverged follows if Congress's re-enacted bar is treated as the deciding action for a congressional ask.
